purpose: Orlistat is used to help people lose weight when combined with a reduced-calorie diet and exercise. It is used in adults and teenagers who are overweight or obese. It can also help keep the weight off once you have lost it.
how_it_works: Orlistat works by blocking some of the fat you eat from being absorbed into your body. It targets an enzyme in your gut called lipase, which normally breaks down fat so your body can use it. Because about one-third of the fat from your meal is not absorbed, those calories pass out of your body instead of being stored.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects involve your stomach and bowels, especially when you eat fatty foods. These include oily or greasy stools, sudden urgent need to use the bathroom, oily spotting on your underwear, gas with oily discharge, and more frequent or loose bowel movements. These side effects are usually manageable and improve over time, especially if you stick to a low-fat diet.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, since rare cases of kidney stones have been reported. This medication can reduce the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, so you should take a multivitamin once a day at least 2 hours before or after your dose. Orlistat can also affect how certain medications are absorbed, including thyroid medicine, blood thinners, and seizure medications, so always tell your doctor and pharmacist all the medicines you take. Do not use it if you are pregnant or have had an organ transplant.
typical_dosing: The prescription strength (Xenical) is typically one 120 mg capsule taken with each main meal that contains fat, up to three times a day. The over-the-counter version (Alli) is one 60 mg capsule with each fat-containing meal, up to three times daily. Take it during the meal or up to one hour after eating. If you skip a meal or eat a meal with no fat, you can skip that dose.
